text.p: Denmark's minority government won massive parliamentary support for its 1997 budget on Thursday after months of political wrangling which at times threatened to topple the centre-left coalition.
Parliament approved the finance bill by 129 votes to seven with both far left and conservative opposition parties backing the balanced budget proposal.
Key to the bill's successful passage and the unpopular government's survival was the support of far left parties holding the balance of power in the 179-seat parliament.
The anti-establishment Unity List abstained after having earlier considered voting against the budget.

The Socialist People's Party (SPP), which has voted against every budget since 1982, backed the 1997 proposal in exchange for government pledges to fund adult education, job retraining, social, environmental and cultural projects and improved workplace conditions.
Financial markets and analysts welcomed the deal, agreed last month, saying that the political stability it promised outweighed concerns about increased left-wing influence on the government.

The opposition Conservatives and Liberals, unable to secure a majority vote against the Social Democrat-led ruling coalition, joined the left on Thursday in voting for the budget at the end of a seven-hour debate in parliament.

The government, vulnerable with only 76 seats to the right-wing opposition's combined 83, began wooing the left after budget talks with the Conservatives collapsed on November 1 over government plans to balance the budget through higher taxes rather than deep spending cuts.
A 0.1 percent rise in gross income tax was passed with leftist support three weeks later.
The government plans to finance the SPP's demands and the eradication of the previously forecast 5.8 billion crown ($973.8 million) budget deficit largely by one-off measures.
One is the liquidation of a state insurance fund against marine war damages estimated to contain some 3.5 billion crowns, built up from premiums from shipowners.
Other funding is to come from the sale of state property holdings and the transfer of money from a workers' holiday fund. ($1=5.956 Danish Crown)
